title: Genitive and dative

objectives.can: Recognise genitive and dative forms and give the commonest sense of each.

explanation.summary: The genitive and the dative are the cases that link a noun to something else in the clause: the genitive most often ties it to another noun ('of'), the dative most often shows to whom, for whom, by what or where. Both are used in more ways than any short rule can cover.

sections.heading: The genitive: 'of'
body: The genitive most often joins one noun to another and is translated with 'of' or with an apostrophe: possession (δοῦλος Χριστοῦ, 'a slave of Christ'), source or origin, a relation (ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου, 'the son of the man'), and the thing described (ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ, 'the love of God').
The genitive also follows many prepositions, such as ἀπό, ἐκ and διά, and a number of verbs. Those uses belong to the preposition or the verb and are learned with it.

sections.heading: The dative: to, for, by, in
body: The dative most often marks the person who receives or benefits: the indirect object, as in ἔδωκεν τοῖς μαθηταῖς, 'he gave to the disciples'. It also very often marks the means or instrument (τῇ χάριτι, 'by grace'), and a place or time (ἐν ὕδατι, 'in water'). A dative may also follow certain prepositions and verbs.

Greek has one dative where other languages have several cases. It stands for the old dative, the instrumental and the locative, which fell together in Greek, and that is why it covers 'to', 'for', 'with', 'by' and 'in'. Context chooses the sense.

sections.heading: Recognising the forms
body: The article helps most: τοῦ and τῆς are genitive singular, τῶν is genitive plural; τῷ and τῇ are dative singular, τοῖς and ταῖς dative plural. The dative singular has an iota, written subscript or as a full letter (λόγῳ, ἀγάπῃ, but also πόλει and ὀνόματι). The genitive singular of the most familiar nouns ends in -ου or -ης or -ας; the genitive plural is regularly -ων.

sections.heading: An example that needs thought
body: ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ may mean the love that God has, the love that God shows, or the love that people have for God. Grammarians call these subjective and objective uses of the genitive, and the Greek phrase does not say which is meant; the surrounding sentence does. In 1 John 4:9 the sentence goes on to speak of God sending his Son, so most readers take it as the love God shows. Do not assume that a genitive always means 'of' in a simple way.

misunderstandings: The genitive is not always 'possession'. 'Of' covers many relations, and some genitives are better rendered with 'from', 'by' or no preposition at all.
The dative is not the case of the direct object. The thing given is accusative; the one who receives it is dative (MAT.14.19: τοὺς ἄρτους accusative, τοῖς μαθηταῖς dative).
Do not learn only one meaning of the dative. 'To' is the most common; 'by', 'with' and 'in' are common too.
Do not decide a case from the ending alone. The same ending can be a different case in another declension, so check the article as well.

deeper.heading: Where the dative's range comes from
body: Indo-European languages kept several separate cases for 'to', 'by or with' and 'at or in'. In Greek the dative, the instrumental and the locative fell together into one form. That history explains why the Greek dative does so many things and why the same ending can be 'to him', 'by it' or 'in it'. In later Greek, the dative gradually gives way to prepositional phrases.

examples.analysis: Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ and θεοῦ are genitives singular masculine. δοῦλος Χριστοῦ Ἰησοῦ is 'a slave of Christ Jesus': the genitive says to whom he belongs. εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ is 'a gospel of God', where the genitive can be read as the gospel that comes from God or that is about him; the phrase itself does not decide.

examples.analysis: ἔδωκεν has a dative and an accusative. τοῖς μαθηταῖς is dative plural, the ones who receive: 'to the disciples'. τοὺς ἄρτους is accusative plural, the thing given. The genitive τοῦ χόρτου follows the preposition ἐπί: 'on the grass'.

examples.analysis: τῇ χάριτι is dative singular feminine: the means, 'by grace'. διὰ πίστεως has a genitive after διά, 'through faith'. The genitive θεοῦ after the preposition ἐκ (in ἐξ … θεοῦ) says where the gift comes from.

examples.analysis: ὕδατι is dative singular neuter, from ὕδωρ. With ἐν it marks the place or the means: 'in water' or 'with water'. The noun's stem changes in the oblique cases; that belongs to a later lesson. For now, notice the dative ending -ι.

examples.analysis: ἡ ἀγάπη τοῦ θεοῦ: τοῦ θεοῦ is genitive singular masculine, 'of God'. Here it is most naturally God's love for us. τὸν υἱὸν αὐτοῦ has a different genitive, αὐτοῦ: 'his Son'. A genitive of the pronoun is the usual way to say 'his', 'her' or 'its'.

practice.explain: ἀνθρώπου is genitive, singular, masculine, from ἄνθρωπος (a man). ἀνθρώπων: genitive, plural; ἀνθρώπῳ: dative, singular; ἀνθρώποις: dative, plural.

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?
practice.explain: ζωῆς is genitive, singular, feminine, from ζωή (life). ζωῇ: dative, singular; νεφελῶν: genitive, plural; καρπῶν: genitive, plural.

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?
practice.explain: ἀναστάσεώς is genitive, singular, feminine, from ἀνάστασις (a rising again, resurrection). ἀναστάσει: dative, singular; κυρίῳ: dative, singular; ἐτῶν: genitive, plural.

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?
practice.explain: γῆς is genitive, singular, feminine, from γῆ (the earth, soil). γῇ: dative, singular; θηρίων: genitive, plural; οὐρανοῖς: dative, plural.

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?
practice.explain: ἐκκλησίας is genitive, singular, feminine, from ἐκκλησία (an assembly, congregation). ἐκκλησίαις: dative, plural; ἐκκλησίᾳ: dative, singular; ἐκκλησιῶν: genitive, plural.

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is genitive, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is dative, singular?

practice.prompt: Which of these is dative, singular?
practice.explain: εἰρήνῃ is dative, singular, feminine, from εἰρήνη (peace, peace of mind). εἰρήνης: genitive, singular; θεοῦ: genitive, singular; στόματος: genitive, singular.
